passages.title: How your Lord destroyed the Army of the Elephant
passages.tafsir:
This passage tells one story: a king marched on Makkah with elephants to pull the Ka'bah down, and Allah destroyed his army with birds. The five ayat move as a single arc — the question in ayah 1 ("Have you not seen…"), the verdict in ayah 2 (their scheme collapsed), the means in ayat 3 and 4 (birds, stones), the outcome in ayah 5 (a field of chewed-up straw). Ibn Kathir names the point: one of the favours Allah did for the Quraysh, saving them from people who "had tried to tear down the Ka'bah and wipe out all traces of its existence."

## "Have you not seen" — to someone who was not there

Ma'arif ul Qur'an flags something easy to miss. The "you" in ayah 1 is the Prophet ﷺ — yet the event happened *before* his blessed birth. He could not have watched it with his own eyes. So why "have you not seen"?

Because, Ma'arif explains, the incident was so widely known that it was as if he ﷺ had seen it himself — and that certainty is what the word *ru'yat* ("seeing") conveys here. Knowledge this public, this uncontested, counts as sight.

Ma'arif adds a haunting detail. Two of Mahmud's drivers — Mahmud was the great elephant — stayed on in Makkah, both of them blind and paralysed. Muhammad Ibn Ishaq reports that Sayyidah 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said she saw them in that state, and her sister Sayyidah Asma' (may Allah be pleased with her) said she saw the two men going around begging. The wreckage of that morning was still limping through the streets a generation later. "In this way," Ma'arif notes, "the traces of this event were seen even after the birth of the Holy Prophet ﷺ" — a momentous event in Arab history, witnessed by hundreds of Arabs.

## The story, as Ibn Kathir tells it

**How Abyssinia came to rule Yemen.** Dhu Nuwas, the last king of Himyar and an idolater, ordered the killing of the People of the Ditch — Christians, roughly twenty thousand of them. A survivor fled to Ash-Sham and sought protection from Caesar, himself a Christian, who wrote to An-Najashi, the king of Abyssinia. An-Najashi sent a great army under two governors, Aryat and Abrahah. Yemen fell; Dhu Nuwas drowned in the sea. The two governors then quarrelled and settled it in single combat: Aryat struck Abrahah across the face with his sword, but 'Atawdah, Abrahah's guard, killed Aryat — and Abrahah, once healed, rose to command the Abyssinian army in Yemen.

**The church meant to replace the Ka'bah.** To win back An-Najashi's favour, Abrahah promised him a church in Yemen the like of which had never been built. He raised a huge structure in San'a', tall and beautifully crafted, decorated (says Ma'arif) with gold, silver and other precious gems. The Arabs called it Al-Qullays because it was so tall that a man tipping his head back to see the top risked his cap falling off. Ma'arif notes that he built it precisely *because* he had witnessed how the Arabs loved the Ka'bah — he wanted their pilgrimage redirected to his building, and proclaimed that no one should visit the Ka'bah in Makkah any more.

This was not a raid for plunder. It was an attempt to relocate the worship of the Arabs.

**The insult.** The proclamation was rejected by the Arab tribes of 'Adnan and Qahtan, and the Quraysh were infuriated by it. Ibn Kathir reports that one of them journeyed to the church, entered it one night and defiled it; its custodians told Abrahah that a Qurayshi had done this "in anger over their House in whose place you have appointed this church."

Ibn Kathir also relays, from Muqatil bin Sulayman, that a group of young men from the Quraysh entered the church and started a fire in it on an extremely windy day, so that it burned and collapsed to the ground. Ma'arif carries a fire in the account too, but a different one: after mentioning the defiling of the church, it says that according to other narratives a nomadic tribe halted near the church and lit a fire for their own needs, the wind that day was blowing violently, and the building caught fire and sustained much loss — and Abrahah, learning of it, understood a Qurayshi to be behind it.

Either way, Abrahah swore to march to the House of Makkah and destroy it stone by stone.

**The march.** An-Najashi sent him, particularly for this expedition, a great and powerful elephant named Mahmud, of a size never seen before. Ibn Kathir adds that it has also been said he had eight other elephants with him, their number also reported as twelve besides Mahmud — "and Allah knows best." The plan was crude and confident: fasten chains to the pillars of the Ka'bah, put the other ends round the elephant's neck, and pull the walls down all at once.

When the Arabs heard, they held it an obligation upon themselves to defend the Sacred House and repel whoever plotted against it. Dhu Nafr, the noblest man of Yemen and greatest of their chiefs, raised an army, fought, lost, and was taken prisoner. Ibn Kathir says plainly that this defeat "was due to Allah's will and His intent to honor and venerate the Ka'bah." Ma'arif puts it more sharply still: it was Allah's will *that no humans should protect His House*. Nufayl bin Habib of Khath'am fought next with his people and was also captured; Abrahah first meant to kill him, then forgave him and pressed him into service as a guide to Al-Hijaz. At Ta'if, the people of Thaqif made terms, anxious for their place of worship, Al-Lat, and sent a guide named Abu Righal. The army settled at Al-Mughammas near Makkah and raided the Makkans' grazing animals — including about two hundred camels belonging to 'Abdul-Muttalib.

## "I am the lord of the camels; the House has its Lord"

Abrahah sent an emissary, Hanatah Al-Himyari, to bring him the head of the Quraysh and to say that the king would not fight the people of Makkah unless they tried to prevent him from destroying the Ka'bah. Hanatah was directed to 'Abdul-Muttalib bin Hashim — the grandfather, Ma'arif notes, of the Prophet ﷺ, and the leader of the Quraysh.

His answer set the tone for all that followed: "By Allah! We have no wish to fight him, nor are we in any position to do so. This is the Sacred House of Allah, and the house of His *Khalil*, Ibrahim… if He lets him approach it, by Allah, we have no means to defend it from him."

Abrahah was impressed by his bearing — 'Abdul-Muttalib was a large and handsome man — and came down from his seat to sit with him on a carpet on the ground. Through his translator he asked what he needed. The reply: *my two hundred camels*.

Abrahah was disgusted. "You are asking me about two hundred camels which I have taken from you and you leave the matter of a house which is (the foundation of) religion and the religion of your fathers, which I have come to destroy?"

Then came the sentence the whole surah turns on. 'Abdul-Muttalib said: **"Verily, I am the lord of the camels. As for the House, it has its Lord Who will defend it."** Abrahah said, "I cannot be prevented." He answered, "Then do so."

Ma'arif explains the logic that puzzles readers here: they spoke to Abrahah about their camels and not about the House of Allah *because they were convinced that Allah's scourge would overtake Abrahah and his troops*. It was not indifference; it was the opposite.

Other chiefs offered Abrahah a third of the wealth of Tihamah to withdraw from the House. He refused — and returned the camels. 'Abdul-Muttalib then ordered the Makkans up into the mountains, took hold of the metal ring on the Ka'bah's door, and called upon Allah along with a number of Quraysh: "There is no matter more important to any man right now than the defense of his livestock and property. So, O my Lord! Defend Your property. Their cross and their cunning will not be victorious over your cunning by the time morning comes."

## The elephant that would not walk

When morning came they mobilised the army and turned Mahmud towards the Ka'bah. Nufayl bin Habib came up, took him by the ear and said: "Kneel, Mahmud! Then turn around and return directly to whence you came. For verily, you are in the Sacred City of Allah." He released the ear, the elephant knelt, and Nufayl hastened away to the mountains.

They beat it on the head with axes and hauled at it with hooked staffs; Ma'arif adds that they struck it with large iron spears and put iron arrowheads in its trunk. It would not rise. They turned it toward Yemen and it stood and walked quickly; toward Ash-Sham, the same; toward the east, the same. Turned back toward Makkah, it knelt down again.

An army that could crush kingdoms could not move one animal a single step in the direction it had come so far to go. Ma'arif calls this "one aspect of the manifestation of the Divine power unfolding itself miraculously."

## Wave after wave: *tayran abābīl*

The other aspect came out of the sky. Ibn Kathir reports that Allah sent against them birds from the sea, like swallows and herons; Ma'arif, describing the same moment, says flocks of birds were seen coming from the sea.

The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites circle the word *abābīl* from different sides, and they converge. Ibn Hisham said it means groups, since the Arabs do not speak of just one bird. Ibn 'Abbas and Ad-Dahhak said "some of them following after others"; Al-Hasan Al-Basri and Qatadah said "many"; Mujahid said "in various, successive groups"; Ibn Zayd said "different, coming from here and there — they came upon them from everywhere." Ishaq bin 'Abdullah bin Al-Harith bin Nawfal, in a report Ibn Jarir records, said it means in divisions, just as camels march in divisions in their herds. Al-Kasa'i heard some grammarians say the singular is *Ibil*; Ma'arif reports that it is a plural said to have no singular at all. So the picture is not one tidy flock but wave after wave, from every direction.

'Ubayd bin 'Umayr described the attack itself: each bird carried three small stones, two in its feet and one in its beak; they came until they gathered in rows over the men's heads, gave a loud cry, and let go what was in their claws and beaks. No stone fell on a man without passing clean through him and out the other side. Then Allah sent a severe wind that struck the stones and increased them in force.

## Stones of *sijjīl* — and what made them lethal

Ibn Hisham reports from Yunus An-Nahwi and Abu 'Ubaydah that in Arab usage *sijjīl* means something hard and solid, and mentions that some commentators hold it to be two Persian words the Arabs fused into one — *Sanj* (stones) and *Jil* (clay). Ma'arif gives the same derivation, from *sang* and *gil*: ordinary, common clay rolled into little balls and then baked hard. Ibn Kathir's narrations describe them as the size of chickpeas and lentils.

Then Ma'arif makes the theological point beautifully. These pebbles were not heavy or hard like rocks chipped off mountains; "they in themselves did not have any devastating power, but it was Allah who created in these stones the high capability" of destruction. The weapon was nothing. The One who wielded it was everything. Ma'arif's opening summary of the surah says it exactly: "Allah destroyed the army with a flock of ordinary birds."

## *Ka-'aṣfin ma'kūl* — an army turned to husk

The closing image is agricultural and deliberately humiliating. Sa'id bin Jubayr said *'asf* means straw — what common people call *Habbūr* — and in another report from him, the leaves of wheat; *al-ma'kūl*, he added, refers to the fodder that is cut for animals, and Al-Hasan Al-Basri said the same. Ibn 'Abbas said *'asf* is the shell of the grain, like the covering of wheat; Ibn Hisham, the leaves of the crops that are not gathered. Ibn Zayd went furthest: the leaves of vegetation and produce, which cattle eat and pass out as dung. Ma'arif adds that chaff is already scattered, and once devoured it does not remain in the same state — "this is what happened to Abrahah and his army."

An imperial army — elephants, a king, a plan years in the making — reduced in one morning to trampled husk. Ibn Kathir sums up ayat 2 and 5 together: Allah "destroyed them, annihilated them and repelled them in their plan and their anger. They did not achieve any good," and not one of them returned to their land to tell of it except that he was wounded. 'Ata' bin Yasar and others said some were destroyed immediately while others were broken down limb by limb as they tried to escape. Abrahah was among the latter; Ibn Ishaq reports that his army carried him back falling apart piece by piece until they reached San'a', where he was like the baby chick of a bird, and he did not die until his heart fell out of his chest — "so they claim," Ibn Kathir adds, an honest flag on what he passes on without vouching for it.

This is what ayah 2 means by their *kayd* — their scheme — being put *fī taḍlīl*: Ibn Kathir renders it "made their plot go astray." The plan did not merely fail; it wandered off, lost its way, and turned on them.

## Why Allah defended idolaters

Ibn Kathir raises the obvious difficulty. Abrahah's men were Christians, and their religion was closer to the true religion than the idolatry of the Quraysh. So why were the idolaters rescued?

His answer is one of the great lines in his tafsir. This was "a means of giving a sign and preparing the way for the coming of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ," for he was born during that same year according to the most popular opinion. And so, he writes, "the tongue of destiny was saying, 'We will not help you, O people of Quraysh, because of any status you may have over the Ethiopians (Abyssinians). We are only helping you in order to defend the Ancient House (the Ka'bah), which We will honor, magnify, and venerate by sending the unlettered Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ, the Finality of all Prophets.'"

The Quraysh were not the point. The House was.

Ma'arif gives this a technical name. A *mu'jizah* — a miracle in the proper sense — is an event Allah brings about to prove a prophet's claim to have been sent by Him, and so comes *after* his divine commission. When a miraculous event comes *before* that claim, the scholars of hadith call it an *irhās*, meaning a prologue or introduction; the word itself means a "foundation stone." Many such events preceded the birth and advent of the Prophet ﷺ, and Ma'arif counts the affair of the People of the Elephant among them. The Year of the Elephant was a foundation stone.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites two hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ invokes this event.

At Al-Hudaybiyyah, as he ﷺ approached the mountain pass leading to the Quraysh, his she-camel knelt and would not rise, and the people said Al-Qaswa' had become stubborn. He ﷺ replied: **"Al-Qaswa' has not become stubborn, for that is not part of her character. Rather, she has been stopped by He Who restrained the Elephant."** He then swore by Him in whose Hand is his soul that the Quraysh would not ask him that day for any term of the treaty in which the sacred things of Allah are honoured without his agreeing to it — and he beckoned the she-camel, and she stood up. Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith is among those Al-Bukhari was alone in recording. The parallel is exact: the same Hand that stopped Mahmud stopped Al-Qaswa', both times for the sanctity of Allah's House.

Then, on the day Makkah was conquered — recorded, Ibn Kathir says, in the Two Sahihs: **"Verily, Allah restrained the Elephant from Makkah, and He has given His Messenger and the believers authority over it. And indeed its sacredness has returned just as it was sacred yesterday. So, let those who are present inform those who are absent."** Abrahah came with elephants and was destroyed; the Prophet ﷺ entered and it was given to him. The difference was never the size of the army.

## What follows, and what it asks of us

Ibn Kathir joins this surah directly to the next: after quoting these five ayat he immediately quotes *"So, let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them against hunger, and has made them safe from fear"* — adding that Allah would not alter the Quraysh's situation, because He wanted good for them if they accepted Him. Ma'arif, citing Qurtubi, fills in what changed on the ground: when Arabia saw that Allah had destroyed their enemy on their behalf, it was convinced that the Quraysh were men under Allah's care and custodians of His Sacred House, and their caravans travelled untouched where others feared highway robbers. And Ibn Ishaq notes that when Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ with prophethood, this defence against the Abyssinians was among the favours he would recount to the Quraysh.

Two things for the reader.

**Ownership clarifies responsibility.** 'Abdul-Muttalib's line is a discipline, not a shrug. He asked for what was genuinely his; what was not his, he entrusted to its Owner — "the House… has its Lord Who will defend it."

**Allah's help does not need your strength, and does not wait on your worthiness.** Dhu Nafr fought and lost. Nufayl fought and lost. The House was defended anyway — by birds, with baked pebbles, on behalf of people who were still idolaters. In ayah 2 the scheme goes astray; by ayah 5 the schemers are husk. And all of it, on the most popular opinion, in the very year the Prophet ﷺ was born — so that the last of the Prophets would open his eyes in a city whose Lord had just shown the peninsula what He does for His House.
